decks.title: Nervous System — Part 1: Neurons, the brain and the spinal cord
goals: Draw and label a neuron and distinguish the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems
State one function of each part of the brain and predict the effect of damage to it
Describe the arrangement of grey and white matter in the brain and spinal cord

slides.heading: Nervous System
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the cells and organs that carry and handle messages in the body.

visual.alt: Flow: a stimulus is detected by a receptor, passed to the brain or spinal cord, and a command goes to an effector, giving a response

slides.narration: Your nervous system is the body's fast messaging service. Sense organs pick up changes, nerves carry messages as electrical impulses, and the brain and spinal cord decide what to do. In this part we meet the nerve cell, the brain and the spinal cord.

slides.heading: Divisions of the nervous system

rows: 12 pairs of cranial and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
Links the CNS with sense organs, muscles and glands
Controls involuntary activities: heartbeat, gut, glands

visual.alt: Table of the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems, what each is made of and its role

slides.narration: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, the control centre. The nerves that spread out from them form the peripheral system. The autonomic system looks after organs we cannot control at will, such as the heart and the gut.

slides.heading: The neuron
slides.body_md: A **neuron** has **dendrites**, a **cell body (cyton)** with a nucleus, and a long **axon** wrapped in a **myelin sheath**.

slides.narration: Dendrites bring impulses in. The cell body keeps the cell alive. The axon carries impulses away, sometimes for a whole metre. Its fatty myelin sheath insulates it and speeds the impulse, which jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next.

slides.heading: Parts of a neuron and the synapse

rows: Receive impulses; carry them to the cell body
Contains the nucleus; controls the cell
Carries impulses away from the cell body
Insulates the axon; speeds the impulse
Release a chemical that carries the impulse across the synapse
Junction between the axon ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a neuron and the synapse, with the job of each

slides.narration: Neurons do not touch one another. At a synapse the axon ending releases a chemical that starts an impulse in the next neuron. Because only axon endings release it, impulses cross synapses in one direction only.

slides.body_md: Fill in: the junction between the axon ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next is a ______.
slides.narration: It begins with the letter s.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how fast is an impulse?
slides.body_md: An impulse travels **1 m** from a toe to the spinal cord.
bullets: Step 1: myelinated fibre at 100 m per s: time = 1 ÷ 100 s = **10 ms**.
Step 2: a fibre without myelin at about 1 m per s: time = **1000 ms**.
Step 3: the myelinated fibre is about **100** times faster.

visual.alt: Worked table: a myelinated fibre at one hundred metres a second takes ten milliseconds; an unmyelinated fibre at one metre a second takes a whole second

slides.narration: Time equals distance divided by speed. A myelinated fibre carries the message from your toe in about a hundredth of a second. Without myelin it would take a whole second, far too slow to save you from a sharp stone.

slides.heading: Three kinds of neuron

rows: From the skin of a finger to the spinal cord
Within the CNS, from sensory to motor neurons
In the grey matter of the spinal cord
From the spinal cord to an arm muscle

visual.alt: Table of sensory, relay and motor neurons with the direction of their impulses and an example

slides.narration: Sensory neurons bring news in. Motor neurons take orders out. Relay neurons, inside the brain and spinal cord, link the two. Remember: sensory in, motor out.

slides.heading: Functions of the parts of the brain

rows: Thinking, memory, intelligence, voluntary actions, sensations
Balance and posture; coordinates muscle movements
Relays sensory impulses to the cerebrum
Body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep; controls the pituitary
Connects parts of the brain; helps regulate breathing
Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing, sneezing

visual.alt: Table of the main functions of the six parts of the brain

slides.narration: Link each part to one clear job. Cerebrum, thinking. Cerebellum, balance. Thalamus, relay station. Hypothalamus, temperature, hunger and thirst. Pons, bridge and breathing. Medulla, the vital centres for heartbeat and breathing.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting the effect of damage
slides.body_md: Work out the function first, then what would be lost.
bullets: Step 1: name the part and its function.
Step 2: say what would happen without that function.
Step 3: check whether the loss is life-threatening.

rows: Breathing or heartbeat may stop: often fatal
Body temperature, hunger or thirst out of control
Loss of memory, speech or voluntary movement

visual.alt: Worked table of four brain parts and the likely effect of damage to each

slides.narration: Effects of damage follow from functions. A blow to the back of the head that harms the cerebellum makes a person stagger. Damage to the medulla is the most dangerous, because breathing and heartbeat depend on it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying actions
slides.body_md: Ask: did it need thinking? Can it be stopped at will? Was it a sudden response to one stimulus?

Step 2: goes on all the time, cannot be stopped → **involuntary**.
Step 3: sudden, automatic response to a stimulus → **reflex**.

Knee kicking when the tendon is tapped

slides.narration: Run through the three questions in order. Answering in class needs thought, so it is voluntary. Peristalsis never stops, so it is involuntary. Coughing at a crumb is sudden and automatic, so it is a reflex.

slides.heading: Spinal and brain reflexes

rows: Knee-jerk; pulling the hand from a hot object
Blinking; narrowing of the pupil in bright light; sneezing

visual.alt: Table of spinal reflexes and reflexes of the brain with examples

slides.narration: Most reflexes of the limbs pass through the spinal cord. Reflexes of the head, such as blinking and the pupil narrowing in bright light, have their centres in the brain. Both are fast and automatic.

slides.heading: Natural and acquired reflexes

rows: Same in all members of a species
Braking at a red light, typing, cycling

visual.alt: Table comparing natural and acquired reflexes

slides.narration: Natural reflexes come with us at birth. Acquired reflexes are learnt. When you first learn to cycle you think about every move, but after practice your feet and hands respond automatically. That is an acquired reflex.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the ruler test
slides.body_md: A ruler is dropped between Nikita's fingers; the distance it falls shows how quickly she reacts.
bullets: Step 1: mean before practice = 18 + 16 + 15 + 17 + 14 ÷ 5 = **16 cm**.
Step 2: mean after practice = 12 + 11 + 13 + 12 + 12 ÷ 5 = **12 cm**.
Step 3: fall in distance = 4 ÷ 16 × 100 = **25%**.

visual.alt: Worked table: mean distance sixteen centimetres before practice and twelve after

slides.narration: Catching the ruler is voluntary: she must see it fall and decide to grip. A shorter distance means a quicker response. With a week of practice the distance fell by a quarter, as the action became more automatic.

slides.heading: How a reflex is learnt

nodes.label: Bell rung each time food is given

visual.alt: Flow of Pavlov's experiment: food causes salivation, a bell is paired with food many times, then the bell alone causes salivation

slides.narration: The scientist Pavlov rang a bell every time he fed a dog. After many repeats the dog salivated at the bell alone. It had learnt to link a new stimulus with food. Such learnt reflexes need the cerebrum.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Voluntary: by will, cerebrum. Involuntary: automatic, medulla and autonomic system. Reflex: sudden, automatic response.
Reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron, effector.
Spinal reflexes pass through the spinal cord; head reflexes through the brain.
Natural reflexes are inborn; acquired reflexes are learnt.

slides.narration: To recap. Actions may be voluntary, involuntary or reflex. A reflex runs along a five-part arc and protects us by its speed. Some reflexes we are born with, and others we learn by practice.

sections.heading: 1. The neuron and the divisions of the nervous system
sections.body_md:
**Neuron (nerve cell):** the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
- **Dendrites:** short branches that **receive** impulses and carry them **towards** the cell body.
- **Cell body (cyton):** contains the **nucleus** and granules; controls the cell.
- **Axon:** a single long fibre carrying impulses **away** from the cell body; covered by a fatty **myelin sheath** (insulates, speeds conduction) broken at **nodes of Ranvier**; ends in branched **axon endings**.
- **Synapse:** the junction between the axon ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next; a **chemical** released by the axon ending carries the impulse across, so impulses pass in **one direction** only.

**Kinds of neuron:** **sensory** (receptor → CNS), **motor** (CNS → effector), **relay** (within the CNS).

| Division | Parts | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Central (CNS)** | Brain and spinal cord | Receives, interprets, decides, commands |
| **Peripheral (PNS)** | 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves | Connects the CNS with receptors and effectors |
| **Autonomic (ANS)** | Nerves to internal organs | Controls involuntary activities: heartbeat, gut, glands, pupil |

sections.heading: 2. The brain
sections.body_md:
The brain lies in the skull (cranium). Its main parts:

| Part | Position | Functions | Effect of damage |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cerebrum** | Largest; two folded hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum | Thinking, memory, intelligence, speech, **voluntary actions**, interpreting sensations | Loss of memory, speech or voluntary movement |
| **Cerebellum** | Back, below the cerebrum | **Balance**, posture, coordination of muscle movements | Staggering, clumsy movements |
| **Thalamus** | Deep in the centre | **Relays** sensory impulses (except smell) to the cerebrum | Disturbed sensations |
| **Hypothalamus** | Below the thalamus | **Body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep**; controls the pituitary | Temperature or appetite out of control |
| **Pons** | Bulge on the brain stem | **Connects** parts of the brain; helps regulate **breathing** | Disturbed breathing |
| **Medulla oblongata** | Lowest part, continues as the spinal cord | **Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure**, swallowing, coughing, sneezing, vomiting | Often fatal |

key_terms.definition_md: Largest part of the brain; thinking and voluntary actions.

sections.heading: 3. The spinal cord; grey and white matter
sections.body_md:
The **spinal cord** runs from the medulla oblongata down through the **vertebral column**, which protects it. It has a **central canal**.
- **Grey matter** = cell bodies of neurons; **white matter** = nerve fibres with white **myelin**.
- In the **cerebrum**: grey matter **outside** (cortex), white matter **inside**.
- In the **spinal cord**: white matter **outside**, grey matter **inside** (butterfly-shaped).

**Functions of the spinal cord:** the white matter **conducts impulses** to and from the brain; the grey matter is the **centre for spinal reflexes**. Spinal nerves leave it through a **dorsal (sensory) root** with a ganglion and a **ventral (motor) root**.

key_terms.definition_md: Nervous tissue made of cell bodies.
Nervous tissue made of myelinated fibres.

sections.heading: 4. Voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions; the reflex arc
sections.body_md:
| Action | Features | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Voluntary** | At will, after thinking; controlled by the **cerebrum**; slower | Writing, walking, speaking |
| **Involuntary** | Not under the will; controlled by the **medulla** and autonomic system | Heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis |
| **Reflex** | Sudden, **automatic** response to a stimulus, without thinking | Knee-jerk, sneezing, coughing, blinking |

**Reflex arc** — the pathway of a reflex: **receptor** → **sensory neuron** → **relay neuron** (grey matter of the spinal cord) → **motor neuron** → **effector** (muscle or gland).
- **Spinal reflexes** (knee-jerk, withdrawal from a hot object) pass through the spinal cord; **reflexes of the brain** (blinking, narrowing of the pupil) through the brain.
- Pain is felt **after** the withdrawal, because the impulse takes longer to reach the brain.
- Reflexes **protect** the body by their speed and leave the brain free for other work.

key_terms.definition_md: Quick, automatic response to a stimulus without thinking.
Pathway of impulses in a reflex action.

sections.heading: 5. Natural and acquired reflexes
sections.body_md:
| Natural (unconditioned) | Acquired (conditioned) |
|---|---|
| Inborn, inherited | Learnt after birth |
| No practice needed | Developed by repeated experience |
| Same in all members of a species | Differ from person to person; may be lost |
| Sneezing, blinking, coughing, a baby sucking, salivation when food is in the mouth | Braking at a red light, typing, cycling, salivation at the sight or smell of a favourite food |

**Pavlov's experiment:** a bell was rung each time a dog was fed. After many repeats the bell alone made the dog salivate — a **conditioned reflex**. Acquired reflexes need the **cerebrum** (learning and memory).

key_terms.definition_md: An inborn reflex needing no learning.
A reflex learnt by repeated experience.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Reversing the direction of the impulse: dendrites carry it **in**, the axon carries it **out**.
- Writing that the cerebrum has grey matter inside: it is the **spinal cord** that has grey matter inside.
- Calling the knee-jerk a voluntary action, or a learnt skill a natural reflex.
- Leaving out the **relay neuron** from a reflex arc.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term (synapse, reflex arc, cyton), a brain part for a function, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: two differences, an effect of damage with its reason.
- 3 marks: a labelled neuron or reflex arc; functions of three brain parts.

questions.stem_md: An impulse crosses a synapse in one direction only, because

options.text_md: only the axon endings release the chemical that carries the impulse across
dendrites have a thicker myelin sheath
the synapse is filled with blood
impulses travel only towards the brain

questions.solution_md: The chemical (neurotransmitter) is stored only in the axon endings, so the message can only pass from axon to the next dendrite — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An impulse travels along a myelinated sensory fibre at about 100 metres per second. How long, in milliseconds, does it take to travel 1 metre from a toe to the spinal cord?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01$ s $= 10$ milliseconds.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Impulses travel faster along myelinated nerve fibres.

**Reason (R):** The myelin sheath is a fatty layer that insulates the axon.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the insulating sheath, broken only at the nodes, lets the impulse jump along quickly — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A nerve impulse passes from the dendrite of one neuron to the axon of the next.

**Reason (R):** At a synapse the impulse is carried across by a chemical.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: the impulse passes from the axon ending of one neuron to the dendrite of the next. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Motor neurons carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to muscles and glands.
questions.solution_md: True. Motor (efferent) neurons carry commands from the CNS to effectors.

questions.stem_md: The functional junction between the axon ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next is called a ______.
questions.solution_md: Synapse.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the part of a neuron that contains the nucleus.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cell body** (cyton).

questions.solution_md: Cyton.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Dendrite, Axon, Nephron, Cyton.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nephron**; the others are **parts of a neuron**.

questions.solution_md: A nephron is a kidney tubule.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems in their roles.

answer.model_answer_md: The **CNS** (brain and spinal cord) receives information, **decides** and sends commands. The **PNS** (cranial and spinal nerves) **links** the CNS with sense organs and muscles. The **autonomic** system controls **involuntary** organs such as the heart, gut and glands.

questions.solution_md: Control centre; connections; involuntary organs.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a neuron. Label the dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon and myelin sheath, and show the direction of the impulse.

answer.model_answer_md: A **cell body** with a **nucleus**, several short branched **dendrites**, a single long **axon** wrapped in **myelin sheath** segments separated by nodes, ending in branched **axon endings**; an **arrow** from the dendrites towards the axon endings.

questions.solution_md: Labelled neuron.

marking_scheme.step: Cell body with nucleus and dendrites
Axon with myelin sheath and endings

questions.stem_md: A man who has drunk too much alcohol staggers and cannot walk in a straight line. The part of his brain most affected is the
questions.solution_md: The cerebellum maintains balance and coordinates muscular movements; alcohol upsets it — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Damage to the medulla oblongata is often fatal because it controls

options.text_md: breathing and the beating of the heart

questions.solution_md: The medulla oblongata contains centres for breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After a head injury, the body temperature of Mr Rao swings between too hot and too cold, and he rarely feels thirsty, though he has no infection. The part of his brain most likely affected is the
questions.solution_md: The hypothalamus, below the thalamus, controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Impulses from the skin, eyes and ears pass through one region deep in the brain before reaching the cerebrum. If this region were damaged, sensations would not reach the cerebrum properly. The region is the
questions.solution_md: The thalamus is the relay centre between the sense pathways (except smell) and the cerebrum — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The pons, a bulge on the brain stem,

options.text_md: connects different parts of the brain and helps to regulate breathing

questions.solution_md: The pons acts as a bridge between parts of the brain and, with the medulla, helps control breathing — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The medulla oblongata controls involuntary actions such as breathing.

**Reason (R):** The medulla oblongata is the largest part of the brain.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: the cerebrum is the largest part; the medulla is small and lowest — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The part of the brain that maintains the balance and posture of the body is the ______.
questions.solution_md: Cerebellum.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Cerebrum, Cerebellum, Spinal nerve, Medulla oblongata.

answer.model_answer_md: **Spinal nerve**; the others are **parts of the brain**.

questions.solution_md: A spinal nerve belongs to the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a severe injury to the medulla oblongata can cause death.

answer.model_answer_md: It controls **breathing and heartbeat**; if these stop, the person dies.

questions.solution_md: Vital centres.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a person under the influence of alcohol often staggers.

answer.model_answer_md: Alcohol affects the **cerebellum**, which maintains **balance** and coordinates movements.

questions.solution_md: Cerebellum affected.

questions.stem_md: Predict one likely effect of damage to (a) the cerebellum and (b) the hypothalamus.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Cerebellum:** loss of **balance** and jerky, **uncoordinated movements**, for example difficulty walking straight.
(b) **Hypothalamus:** failure to control **body temperature**, or disturbed **hunger, thirst** or sleep.

questions.solution_md: Balance; temperature or hunger.

questions.stem_md: State one function each of the cerebrum, the thalamus and the pons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cerebrum:** centre of **thinking, memory, intelligence** and **voluntary actions**; it also interprets sensations.
2. **Thalamus:** **relays sensory impulses** to the cerebrum (and gives a rough sense of pain).
3. **Pons:** **connects** different parts of the brain and helps **regulate breathing**.

questions.solution_md: One function each.

questions.stem_md: In a transverse section of the spinal cord,

options.text_md: grey matter lies inside and white matter outside
grey matter lies outside and white matter inside

questions.solution_md: The spinal cord has a butterfly of grey matter in the centre with white matter round it, the reverse of the cerebrum — option (a).

questions.stem_md: White matter looks white because it consists mainly of

options.text_md: nerve fibres covered by myelin sheaths

questions.solution_md: The fatty myelin sheaths of the fibres give white matter its colour; grey matter is mostly cell bodies — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which pair gives two functions of the spinal cord?

options.text_md: It stores memory, and it controls hunger
It pumps blood, and it filters lymph
It carries impulses to and from the brain, and it is a centre for many reflex actions
It makes hormones, and it controls balance

questions.solution_md: The white matter conducts impulses up and down; the grey matter coordinates spinal reflexes — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The outer part of the spinal cord is white.

**Reason (R):** It consists mainly of nerve fibres covered by myelin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the white myelin of the fibres is why the outer part looks white — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the cerebrum, grey matter lies inside and white matter lies outside.
questions.solution_md: False. In the cerebrum grey matter forms the outer cortex and white matter lies inside; the spinal cord has the reverse.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: white matter of the brain and spinal cord appears white.

answer.model_answer_md: It is made of nerve fibres covered by **white, fatty myelin sheaths**.

questions.solution_md: Myelin.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the arrangement of grey and white matter differs between the cerebrum and the spinal cord.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **cerebrum**, **grey matter** (cell bodies) forms the **outer cortex** and **white matter** (myelinated fibres) lies **inside**. In the **spinal cord** the arrangement is **reversed**: grey matter is **inside**, shaped like a butterfly, and white matter is **outside**.

questions.solution_md: Reversed arrangement.

questions.stem_md: A reflex action is

options.text_md: an action done after careful thought
an action controlled only by hormones
a quick, automatic response to a stimulus, made without thinking
a slow growth movement towards light

questions.solution_md: Reflexes are rapid, involuntary responses that do not need a conscious decision — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which sequence shows the path of an impulse in a reflex arc?

options.text_md: Effector → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → receptor
Receptor → motor neuron → brain → sensory neuron → effector
Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Sensory neuron → receptor → effector → motor neuron → relay neuron

questions.solution_md: The impulse starts at the receptor, goes in by the sensory neuron, crosses a relay neuron in the spinal cord and leaves by the motor neuron to the effector — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a voluntary action?

options.text_md: Sneezing when pepper enters the nose
Writing a letter to a friend
Pulling the hand away from a thorn

questions.solution_md: Writing is done at will and is controlled by the cerebrum; the others happen without thought — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When the tendon below the kneecap is tapped, the leg kicks forward. This knee-jerk is

options.text_md: a voluntary action controlled by the cerebrum
an acquired reflex learnt in childhood
a reflex controlled by the spinal cord
an action of the autonomic system on the heart

questions.solution_md: The knee-jerk is a spinal reflex: the arc passes through the spinal cord without needing the brain — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Kiran blinks when a cricket ball suddenly comes towards her face. This is

options.text_md: a reflex action controlled by the brain
a reflex controlled only by the spinal cord
an involuntary action of the heart

questions.solution_md: Blinking is a reflex; its centre lies in the brain, as the eyes are served by cranial nerves (a cranial reflex) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of a reflex arc, which letter marks the neuron that lies wholly inside the spinal cord?
questions.solution_md: C is the relay neuron in the grey matter. A is the receptor, B the sensory neuron, D the motor neuron — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The sensory nerve fibres from Ravi's left hand are cut where they enter the spinal cord, but the motor fibres are intact. If his left hand touches a hot iron, he will

options.text_md: feel the heat but be unable to move the hand
pull the hand away but not feel the heat
feel the heat and pull the hand away as usual
neither feel the heat nor pull the hand away by reflex

questions.solution_md: Without the sensory pathway, no impulse reaches the spinal cord or brain, so there is no sensation and no reflex, although the muscles could still work if commanded — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A reflex action is quicker than a voluntary action.

**Reason (R):** All reflex actions are present from birth.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true: a spinal reflex need not wait for the brain to decide. The reason is false: acquired reflexes are learnt after birth — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the pathway followed by an impulse from a receptor to an effector in a reflex action.

answer.model_answer_md: **Reflex arc.**

questions.solution_md: Reflex arc.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the neuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord that links the sensory neuron with the motor neuron.

answer.model_answer_md: **Relay neuron** (intermediate or association neuron).

questions.solution_md: Relay neuron.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Sneezing, Coughing, Knee-jerk, Painting a picture.

answer.model_answer_md: **Painting a picture**; the others are **reflex actions**.

questions.solution_md: Painting is a voluntary action.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: we pull our hand away from a hot object before we feel any pain.

answer.model_answer_md: The withdrawal is a **spinal reflex**: the spinal cord sends the command at once, while the impulse for **pain** takes longer to reach the **brain**.

questions.solution_md: Spinal reflex is faster.

marking_scheme.step: Reflex through the spinal cord before the brain registers pain

questions.stem_md: State two differences between a voluntary action and a reflex action.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A voluntary action is done **at will**, after **thinking**; a reflex action is **automatic**, without thinking.
2. A voluntary action is controlled by the **cerebrum** and is slower; a reflex is usually controlled by the **spinal cord** and is very **quick**.

questions.solution_md: Will; control centre; speed.

questions.stem_md: Describe the path of the impulse when you step on a sharp pin and lift your foot at once.

answer.model_answer_md: The **receptor** in the skin of the sole is stimulated. The impulse travels along a **sensory neuron** to the **spinal cord**, where a **relay neuron** in the grey matter passes it to a **motor neuron**. The motor neuron carries it to the **leg muscles** (effector), which contract and lift the foot.

questions.solution_md: Receptor, sensory, relay, motor, effector.

marking_scheme.step: Relay neuron in the spinal cord

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a reflex arc through the spinal cord. Label the receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector.

answer.model_answer_md: A **transverse section** of the spinal cord with **grey matter inside**; a **sensory neuron** from a **receptor** in the skin entering by the dorsal side (cell body in a ganglion); a **relay neuron** in the grey matter; a **motor neuron** leaving by the ventral side to a **muscle (effector)**; arrows showing the direction.

questions.solution_md: Labelled reflex arc.

marking_scheme.step: Spinal cord section with grey matter
Receptor, effector and labels with arrows

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a natural (unconditioned) reflex?

options.text_md: Stopping a bicycle on seeing a red light
Sneezing when dust enters the nose
Reaching for a mobile phone when it rings

questions.solution_md: Sneezing is inborn and needs no learning; the others are learnt through practice — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an acquired (conditioned) reflex?

options.text_md: Blinking when an insect flies near the eye
The knee-jerk when the tendon is tapped
Coughing when food goes down the wrong way
A cyclist braking at once on seeing a red traffic light

questions.solution_md: Braking at a red light is learnt by repeated experience; the others are inborn reflexes — option (d).

children.stem_md: Name the rounded part labelled B.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cell body** (cyton).

children.stem_md: Name A and C and state the direction in which each carries impulses.

answer.model_answer_md: **A: dendrites**, which carry impulses **towards** the cell body. **C: axon**, which carries impulses **away from** the cell body.

marking_scheme.step: A dendrites, towards the cell body
C axon, away from the cell body

children.stem_md: Name D and state its function.

answer.model_answer_md: D is the **myelin sheath**, a fatty covering of the axon. It **insulates** the axon and makes the impulse travel **faster**.

children.stem_md: What happens at E when an impulse arrives?

answer.model_answer_md: E are the **axon endings**. The impulse makes them **release a chemical**, which crosses the **synapse** and starts an impulse in the **dendrites of the next neuron** (or in a muscle).

marking_scheme.step: Crosses the synapse to the next neuron

children.stem_md: Many fibres like C, covered by D, make up white matter. Explain why white matter is white, and state where it lies in the cerebrum and in the spinal cord.

answer.model_answer_md: White matter is white because its nerve fibres are covered with **white, fatty myelin**. In the **cerebrum** it lies **inside**, beneath the grey cortex; in the **spinal cord** it lies **outside**, around the grey matter.

children.solution_md: Myelin; inside cerebrum, outside spinal cord.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Just before a board examination, Arnav's heart pounded, his mouth felt dry and his palms became sweaty. He tried to calm down, but he could not stop these changes by willing them to stop. Then he picked up his pen and began to write.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **autonomic nervous system**.

**(b)** They take place **automatically**, without Arnav's **will** or conscious control; he could **not stop** them by deciding to, because they are not controlled by the cerebrum.

**(c)** The **central** nervous system is the **brain and spinal cord**, which receive information and **decide** responses. The **peripheral** system is the **cranial and spinal nerves**, which **connect** the CNS with the sense organs, muscles and glands.

**(d)** Any two: the **movements of the stomach and intestine** (peristalsis), the **secretion** of saliva and digestive juices, the **size of the pupil**, the rate of **breathing**.

**(e)** (i) **Voluntary:** picking up his pen and **writing**.
(ii) **Involuntary:** his **heart pounding** (or sweating).
(iii) **Reflex:** **blinking** if something came near his eyes, or pulling his hand away from a sharp pen nib.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Autonomic.

**(b)** Not under the will.

**(c)** Brain and spinal cord vs nerves.

**(d)** Gut movements, secretion, pupil.

**(e)** Writing; heartbeat; blinking.

answer.model_answer_md: The **central** nervous system is the **brain and spinal cord**, which receive information and **decide** responses. The **peripheral** system is the **cranial and spinal nerves**, which **connect** the CNS with the sense organs, muscles and glands.
